items.direction: Narrate this as a high-energy, feel-good YouTube video counting down eight Vietnam facts that sound fake but are real. The Narrator is THRILLED and grinning the whole time: an excited, fun friend who just found out these facts about Vietnam and is bursting to tell you. Huge smile you can hear in every line, bright and upbeat, warm and natural like real excited conversation, never like reading a script. Wide, lively pitch movement; real amazement on every number and reveal; playful delighted laughter in the voice on the funny bits (thirty million people all called Nguyen, you can read it but you just can't say it, grandmas and whole families on one scooter, a little bit of Vietnam in your morning jar, 'and yes, he was a Nguyen, of course he was', a brand-new ruin, just like a unicorn nobody has seen one, a man hiding from the weather). The three tones of 'ma' (ghost, mother, horse) are said playfully, with a beat between each. The story of the lost cave in number one is told like a gripping campfire story, building up, then pure wonder at the size. The opening bet is a cheeky, confident challenge with a grin, and so is the closing 'do you owe me a hundred dollars'. Punch the key words with energy. Pace quick and bouncy, about 170 words per minute, short crisp pauses; never flat, calm, sleepy, monotone or documentary-serious, and never shouty or fake. Accent: native General American English, neutral American accent from first word to last. VOICE IDENTITY: the same person and the same high energy from the first line to the last. Pronounce 'Vietnam' as 'vee-et-NAHM', 'Vietnamese' as 'vee-et-nah-MEEZ', 'Nguyen' as 'NWIN', 'Nguyen Van Giang' as 'NWIN vahn ZAHNG', 'Hanoi' as 'ha-NOY', 'Ho Chi Minh City' as 'hoh chee MIN city', 'Quang Binh' as 'kwahng BIN', 'Da Nang' as 'dah NAHNG', 'Laos' as 'LAH-ohs', 'saola' as 'sow-LAH', 'robusta' as 'roh-BUS-tuh', 'Metropole' as 'MET-roh-pole', 'Ha Long' as 'hah LONG', 'Ho Khanh' as 'hoh KAHN', 'Son Doong' as 'sun DOONG', 'tiramisu' as 'teer-uh-mee-SOO', 'fibreglass' as 'FY-ber-glass'. Read ONLY the text provided, word for word: stop right after the final sentence and never add, invent or continue with any words of your own. The text is given one sentence group per line: read every line in order, do not skip any line.
lines: I bet you a hundred dollars you can't guess how many people in Vietnam share the same last name.
By some counts, it's close to four in ten. That's more than thirty million people, all called Nguyen.
This country has an animal that no scientist has ever seen in the wild.
A bridge held up by two giant hands.
And a cave so big, it makes its own weather.
Every single one is real. And they get crazier as we go.
Grab a map of Vietnam. Here are eight facts nobody believes. Starting with number eight.
Number eight. You can already read Vietnamese.
Well, sort of. Look at a street sign in Hanoi, and you'll see the same A, B, C you're reading right now.
Its neighbours, China, Laos and Cambodia, all use their own scripts. Vietnam uses Latin letters.
For centuries, Vietnamese was written with Chinese characters.
Then in the sixteen hundreds, European missionaries wrote the language down using the alphabet they knew.
And in 1910, under French rule, that alphabet was made compulsory.
But here's the catch. Those little marks above the letters change the meaning.
Say "ma" one way, and it means ghost. Another way, mother. Another way, horse.
So you can read Vietnamese. You just can't say it.
And if you think the language moves fast, wait till you see the traffic.
Number seven. Vietnam has more than eighty-four million registered motorbikes.
The whole country has about a hundred and two million people. That's more than four bikes for every five people.
Kids, grandmas, entire families, all riding on one scooter.
At rush hour in Ho Chi Minh City, the roads stop looking like traffic and start looking like a river of helmets.
Crossing the street is a skill. You walk slowly and steadily, and the bikes flow around you.
And all those riders run on one fuel. Not petrol. Coffee.
Number six. Vietnam is the world's second-biggest coffee producer. Only Brazil grows more.
It grows around forty percent of the world's robusta beans. The strong, bitter kind that goes into a lot of instant coffee.
So there's a good chance your morning jar has a little bit of Vietnam in it.
But the craziest part is how they drink it. With eggs.
In 1946, Hanoi ran short of milk. So a bartender at the Metropole Hotel, named Nguyen Van Giang, whisked egg yolks and sugar into a thick, sweet foam.
He spooned it on top of strong coffee, and egg coffee was born.
People say it tastes like tiramisu in a cup. And yes, he was a Nguyen. Of course he was.
Now, to try egg coffee in every corner of Vietnam, you'd have to cover a very strange shape.
Number five. Vietnam is shaped like a giant letter S.
From top to bottom, it stretches about one thousand, six hundred and fifty kilometres.
But at its narrowest point, in Quang Binh province, it's only about fifty kilometres wide.
Long enough that flying from Hanoi to Ho Chi Minh City takes about two hours. Narrow enough to drive across in about one.
Stand on the beach there, and Laos is just over the mountains behind you.
And further south, up in those same mountains, someone built a bridge for giants.
Number four. Near Da Nang, about fourteen hundred metres above the sea, there's a bridge held up by two giant stone hands.
It's called the Golden Bridge. It's a hundred and fifty metres long, and it curves right through the clouds.
The hands look ancient. Cracked, mossy, like they've been holding it for a thousand years.
They haven't. The bridge opened in 2018.
And the hands aren't even stone. They're a wire frame covered in fibreglass, painted to look old.
A brand-new ruin. And number three is the opposite. Something ancient that we only just found.
Number three. In 1992, scientists surveying a forest in Vietnam spotted a strange skull in a hunter's home.
It had two long, straight horns. And it belonged to an animal science had never described. The saola.
A brand-new large mammal, discovered in the nineteen nineties. That almost never happens.
People call it the Asian unicorn. Because just like a unicorn, almost nobody has seen one.
No scientist has ever reported seeing a saola alive in the wild. The last known photo came from a hidden camera, in 2013.
There may be fewer than a hundred left. Hiding somewhere in these forests right now.
And if that animal is hard to find, number two has almost two thousand places to hide.
One thousand, nine hundred and sixty-nine islands, rising straight out of the sea.
Limestone towers, packed into about fifteen hundred square kilometres of water.
Its name means "where the dragon descends".
Legend says a family of dragons came down to protect Vietnam from invaders, and spat out jewels that became these islands.
Today it's a UNESCO World Heritage Site. And honestly, it looks like a planet from a sci-fi movie.
But the islands are only the outside. To find the craziest thing in Vietnam, you have to go underground.
Number one. In 1990, a local man named Ho Khanh was deep in the jungle when a storm hit.
He ran for shelter under a cliff. And there, he felt something strange. Wind, blowing out of the ground. And the sound of a river, far below.
It was the entrance to a cave. But the drop inside was too steep, so when the storm passed, he left.
And then he couldn't find it again.
For eighteen years, the entrance stayed lost. Until 2008, when he finally found it, and marked the trail.
In 2009, a British caving team went inside. And what they found was the biggest cave passage on Earth. Son Doong.
In places, it's about two hundred metres high, and one hundred and fifty metres wide.
You could fit a forty-storey building inside. People say a jumbo jet could fly through parts of it.
Where the roof has collapsed, sunlight pours in. And down there, there's a jungle. Trees over forty metres tall, growing inside a cave.
It has its own river. And it's so huge, it makes its own clouds.
A cave with its own weather. Found by a man hiding from the weather.
So, did you believe all eight? Or do you owe me a hundred dollars?
And which country should we do next? Tell us in the comments.
On this channel, we take the places you think you know and show you what's really there.
So if you want the next one, subscribe. It costs a lot less than a hundred dollars.
See you in the next country.
